title: Common technology providers can turn isolated bank disruptions into shared financial risk
summary: The ECB’s financial stability special feature argues that widespread AI adoption could make operational failures at different banks more correlated. A single institution can benefit from the expertise of a large technology provider while the system as a whole becomes more dependent on that provider. If several banks rely on the same service and cannot substitute another at short notice, disruption can impair payments or other important functions across institutions. The authors distinguish this possibility from the record to date. The euro area banking system had experienced no systemic cyber event by the November 2026 publication (Sections 1 and 3).

For a local incident to become systemic, it must exhaust the capacity of institutions and markets to absorb disruption. The feature identifies operational, financial and confidence channels. A service can be interrupted, an institution can suffer a loss or face a need for liquidity, and customers or counterparties can lose confidence. Interconnectedness, substitution options and common exposures help determine whether any of those effects spreads. The initial problem could originate with an external infrastructure provider or in the real economy. The number of individual incidents alone therefore says little about how close the financial system has come to losing a critical function (Section 1).

The evidence combines different types of observations. Chart B.1 counts publicly disclosed incidents, whose coverage changed in 2023 and whose reporting can be delayed. Its full-year 2026 estimate is an extrapolation. Chart B.6 combines a survey of financial firms’ risk concerns with the frequency of topics discussed in the earnings calls of 82 banks. Those measures capture incident visibility, perceived risk and management attention, respectively. Chart B.7 instead uses major incident reports collected under the Digital Operational Resilience Act from the first quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026. Malicious actions accounted for a relatively small share, and most recorded incidents had limited impact. Neither the historic loss record nor increased attention in earnings calls supplies an estimate of future systemic losses.

The short-term concern is uneven capacity to adjust. More capable models can improve defensive work, but financial firms must validate changes and maintain services while implementing them. A small firm may struggle with fixed costs that a specialist service provider can share across many customers. Access to leading technology also varies across countries. In an EBA survey, 56% of banks in the first half of 2026 reported no attacks that had caused or could have caused a major ICT incident, up from 49% in the previous half. At the opposite end, the share reporting eleven or more increased from 7% to 11%. Both ends rose. The authors call that possible early evidence of divergence, without attributing the survey change solely to AI (Sections 2–3).

The feature presents the balance of future costs and benefits as uncertain. Better tools could improve how quickly financial institutions respond, while greater reliance on automation could make some functions harder to perform manually during an outage. More concentrated infrastructure could strengthen individual providers’ capabilities while reducing the banking system’s alternatives. The authors favour collective contingency planning, regular testing across organisations, mapping critical service dependencies and cooperation between banks, providers and public authorities. Existing European rules address aspects of governance and third-party concentration. Their implementation and the ability of several institutions to recover together matter more for the systemic question than whether an individual firm reports a low recent loss (Section 4).

questions.question: Which critical services can affected banks actually restore independently?
questions.detail: The feature identifies concentration among external providers, but a vendor count alone does not show whether multiple providers depend on the same underlying infrastructure. Compare critical-function registers, recovery objectives and joint contingency exercise results. The time required to restore a payment or settlement service would help assess whether common outsourcing creates a material liquidity exposure.

questions.question: Do the two tails of the bank survey reflect different financial vulnerabilities?
questions.detail: More banks reported no qualifying attacks while more reported at least eleven. The feature treats this as possible divergence. Comparable supervisory reporting would need to distinguish differences in detection, size, business model and service dependencies from changes in actual disruption. Investors could then assess whether a higher incident count predicts downtime or costs, or chiefly indicates better visibility.

questions.question: When could a service interruption generate a funding need before recovery?
questions.detail: Operational losses can be modest while a delay in payments or loss of confidence produces a need for cash. The feature sets out the possible channels without quantifying them. Examine the timing of missed obligations, backup arrangements, liquid resources and customer responses in documented incidents and supervisory exercises. Those observations would help separate short-lived inconvenience from a threat to several institutions’ financial commitments.
